segment_name: Identity / Security / Zero Trust / Cross-Domain Infrastructure
what_it_does: This layer decides WHO (person or non-person entity) may touch WHICH data or service, under WHAT policy, and HOW data may cross security or national boundaries. It spans: (1) identity, credential and access management (DoD PKI/CAC, enterprise directories such as DISA's Global Federated User Directory, Army Enterprise ICAM, MFA, non-person-entity certificates); (2) zero-trust access and enforcement (policy decision/enforcement points, ZTNA/SASE, micro-segmentation; DoD's 7 pillars, 45 capabilities and 152 activities of which 91 are 'target level' due by FY27); (3) authorization and policy engines (RBAC to ABAC using user, device and data attributes); (4) data-centric security and tagging (classification/releasability labels, IC-TDF -> OpenTDF/ZTDF, ACP-240 coalition labels, key-access services) so protection travels with the object; (5) cross-domain solutions (NSA/NCDSMO-baselined transfer and access guards, one-way transfer devices, tactical CDS) that move data between classification levels or coalition enclaves; and (6) coalition identity federation and foreign-disclosure/releasability enforcement in Mission Partner Environments. In the C4ISR chain it is cross-cutting: it gates every TRANSPORT, PROCESS, FUSE and DISSEMINATE_TASK hop, and it is the reason 'the data exists but cannot be shared' is the most common C4ISR failure mode documented in exercises.

sub_taxonomy.name: Enterprise ICAM (PKI/CAC/PIV, derived credentials, MFA, directories, NPE identity, federation)
sub_taxonomy.note: DoD PKI + DISA GFUD/DEAS + service ICAM programs (Army EICAM, Navy Flank Speed/Entra). Largely commoditized by Microsoft/hyperscaler identity stacks; still manual for coalition/guest identities. Restructured from the assignment's 'credentialing' bullet to include NPE (machine) identity because ZT strategy and NGC2 make device/sensor identity the growth edge.

sub_taxonomy.name: Zero-trust access/network enforcement (ZTNA, SASE, segmentation, policy enforcement points)
sub_taxonomy.note: Thunderdome (DISA/Fourth Estate), Flank Speed (Navy), service SD-WAN/SASE deployments; production stage; dominated by Booz Allen, Microsoft, Zscaler-class vendors. Not startup whitespace.

sub_taxonomy.name: Authorization / policy engines (PDP, ABAC, dynamic and risk-based access)
sub_taxonomy.note: The DoD ZT 'Data' and 'User' pillars require ABAC; DAU webinars from 2023 (ABAC) to 2026 (ICAM powers ZT) show components still migrating from RBAC to ABAC. Accessible to software startups (OPA/Cedar/OpenTDF-style engines) but integration-heavy.

sub_taxonomy.name: Data-centric security and tagging/labeling (TDF/ZTDF/OpenTDF, IC-TDF, ACP-240, markings, key access services)
sub_taxonomy.note: Recurring DoD CIO ZT PfMO topic (data tagging webinars Apr 2024, Sep 2025). Open standards exist (OpenTDF spec, ZTDF for Five Eyes/NATO) but tagging of live C2 data at source is nascent. Most accessible sub-problem for an unclassified prototype.

sub_taxonomy.name: Cross-domain solutions (transfer/access guards, one-way transfer, tactical/low-SWaP CDS, CDS-as-a-service)
sub_taxonomy.note: Governed by DoDI 8540.01, CNSSI 1253 CDS overlay and NSA/NCDSMO 'Raise the Bar'; only NCDSMO-listed products may be used (NIST AC-4(20)). Incumbent oligopoly (Everfox, Owl, GDMS, Northrop, Lockheed Radiant Mercury); immediately classified and export-controlled.

sub_taxonomy.name: Coalition identity federation and releasability enforcement (MPE ICAM, foreign disclosure workflow, NOFORN/REL handling)
sub_taxonomy.note: Joint Staff J6 and DISA are still demonstrating ZT + data-centric security for partners beyond FVEY (FY27 justification book); MPE remains 'network-centric' until ~2027 per DISA. Policy-bound and classified at the edges but with unclassified workflow/tooling openings.

sub_taxonomy.name: Tactical / DDIL zero trust (edge PDP, offline credential validation, data-in-use protection)
sub_taxonomy.note: Added because DEVCOM C5ISR's 2025 'Tactical Data in Use Security' RFI explicitly asks for ZT Data-pillar capabilities that work in DDIL; enterprise ZT designs assume connectivity to identity providers and key servers.

current_architecture.description: Enterprise identity is anchored on DoD PKI (CAC/PIV, NPE certificates) and enterprise directories (DISA GFUD/DEAS; service Active Directory/Entra tenants such as Navy Flank Speed). Zero-trust enforcement is delivered as SASE/ZTNA overlays (Thunderdome for DISA and the Fourth Estate; hyperscaler-native conditional access for Flank Speed) with policy decision points that are still largely role-based and network-centric outside the leading programs. Data-centric security exists as standards (IC-TDF, OpenTDF, ZTDF, ACP-240) and pilots rather than as enterprise-wide tagging at source. Movement across classification levels and to coalition partners runs through a small set of NCDSMO-baselined cross-domain solutions (enterprise CDES at DISA; program-specific guards such as BICES TNE; tactical CDS on aircraft, vehicles and expeditionary nodes), with manual review, removable media and liaison officers as the fallback. Coalition access uses separate enclaves (CENTRIXS, BICES, MPE/Coalition Information Environment) rather than federated identity with attribute-based release.

current_architecture.security_domain: Spans unclassified (NIPR/IL2-IL5), Secret (SIPR/IL6), TS/SCI and coalition Secret-REL enclaves; the segment's core products (CDS, CSfC) are by definition multi-domain and immediately classified/export-controlled, while tagging, policy and observability tooling can be built unclassified.
current_architecture.connectivity_dependency: Enterprise ZT and ICAM assume reachability of identity providers, policy decision points, certificate revocation services and key access servers; Flank Speed and Thunderdome are cloud/enterprise-hosted. Tactical CDS are local hardware, but their filter updates and audit offload assume periodic connectivity.
current_architecture.what_breaks_when_disconnected: Token/certificate validation, attribute retrieval and key release fail or fall back to cached trust; users lose access to cloud identity services; data tagged for ABAC cannot be decrypted without key servers; cross-domain transfers revert to manual/removable-media processes. DEVCOM C5ISR's 2025 RFI for 'Tactical Data in Use Security' in DDIL is direct government acknowledgement of this gap.

technical_difficulty.summary: Bimodal. The enterprise half (SSO, ZTNA, conditional access, directories) is commodity engineering assembled from hyperscaler and vendor components; the differentiator is integration, accreditation and scale, not novel technology. The hard half is (a) high-assurance cross-domain filtering that must satisfy Raise the Bar (redundant, independent, always-invoked, non-bypassable filter pipelines, normalized-format regeneration) and pass NSA lab assessment; (b) consistent attribute semantics across federated authorities (DoD, services, coalition) so that ABAC decisions are the same everywhere; (c) automated releasability decisions where markings do not aggregate by dominance (any NOFORN element blocks foreign release); and (d) making ZT work when the identity provider, PDP and key server are unreachable (DDIL).
required_expertise: Policy engines and ABAC modeling (OPA/Rego, Cedar, XACML lineage)
Cryptography and key management (TDF/ZTDF key access services, HSMs, CNSA 2.0)
High-assurance systems engineering, formal methods and separation kernels for CDS
Content filtering, data format descriptions (DFDL), USMTF/CoT/Link-16 message schemas
Classification and foreign disclosure policy (DoDM 5200.01, CAPCO, ACP-240, NATO STANAG labels)
DevSecOps and cATO evidence automation (NIST 800-53 rev5, ZT Overlays)
Tactical networking and offline-first distributed systems
technical_difficulty.hardest_problem: Getting an automated, policy-consistent releasability and access decision on machine-generated tactical data (tracks, reports, video) across US-only, coalition and partner enclaves without a human in the loop, while satisfying NCDSMO assurance requirements and surviving disconnection. Today this is solved by people, liaison officers and regeneration workarounds.
technical_difficulty.commodity_parts: Identity providers, MFA, ZTNA/SASE, SIEM, OPA/Cedar policy engines, OpenTDF SDKs and key access server, Kubernetes with policy-as-code, FedRAMP/IL5 hosting via Game Warden or hyperscalers.

capital_intensity.first_production_deployment_usd: $3M-$15M for software tooling (tagging/policy/observability); $10M-$40M and 3-5 years if the product itself must become an NCDSMO-baselined CDS
capital_intensity.assumptions: PoC assumes two founders building on OpenTDF/OPA with synthetic or unclassified C2 data (CoT, USMTF samples). Credible demo assumes an SBIR Phase I/II or xTech award, IL4/IL5 hosting through an accredited intermediary, DoD PKI test credentials, and participation in an Army/Joint experiment (T-REX, Project Convergence, Bold Quest) with a government sponsor such as DEVCOM C5ISR. First production assumes ATO/cATO on a service enclave, FedRAMP High or IL5 reciprocity, 3-6 cleared or clearable staff, and 18-36 months. CDS route assumes NSA lab-based security assessment, hardware/software development to RTB, and export-control compliance; incumbents' sole-source IDIQs show the buyer will not run new competitions frequently.

regulatory_access.prototype_with_commercial_unclassified_d: yes for data tagging, policy engines, ZT observability and ICAM integration tooling (OpenTDF, synthetic CoT/USMTF); no for cross-domain solutions and CSfC-type products, which have no meaningful unclassified market and require NSA processes
regulatory_access.government_data_required: Not for a first prototype; needed for credibility: DoD PKI test certificates, sample marked data and access to a service enclave, typically via SBIR/OTA sponsor or an exercise.
regulatory_access.itar_ear: CDS and high-assurance guards are treated as export-controlled (NSA RTB explicitly covers 'all cross domain solutions being sold for export'); encryption products fall under EAR Cat. 5 Part 2 and may be USML-controlled when designed for military use; tagging/policy software built on open standards can be EAR99 or 5D002 depending on crypto. Needs export-control counsel before any foreign-national access to controlled technical data.
regulatory_access.cui_likely: yes; any real customer data (attributes, network topology, marking rules) will be CUI at minimum and drive CMMC Level 2 obligations
regulatory_access.classified_integration_eventually: yes for anything touching SIPR, coalition Secret-REL or CDS; the segment's value concentrates at classification boundaries
regulatory_access.cleared_personnel_at_mvp: no for unclassified tooling MVP; yes (Secret at minimum, often TS/SCI) for CDS, CSfC integration, coalition MPE work and most production deployments
regulatory_access.non_us_person_founder_note: An Indonesian citizen without U.S. person status cannot hold a U.S. security clearance and generally may not access ITAR-controlled technical data or export-controlled encryption source without licenses; a company with a foreign owner/officer may raise FOCI questions in facility clearance and some SBIR eligibility contexts. A German founder who becomes a lawful permanent resident is a 'U.S. person' for ITAR/EAR deemed-export purposes but still cannot hold a clearance until naturalized. Practical implication: structure the company so the non-U.S.-person founder owns product/business functions on unclassified, non-export-controlled work, keep controlled technical data segregated, and obtain specialist immigration, export-control and FOCI legal review before pursuing CDS, CSfC or classified integration. This is a description of constraints, not legal advice.

why_not_solved.explanation: Any product that moves data across classification boundaries must pass NSA/NCDSMO lab-based assessment against Raise the Bar and be listed before use (NIST AC-4(20)); CSfC components need NIAP validation and a trusted integrator. This takes years and specialized staff, which is why the CDS market is an oligopoly.
The highest-value use cases (SIPR, coalition Secret-REL, TS/SCI) require cleared people, facilities and government-furnished environments; startups cannot iterate with real data.
Everfox, Owl, GDMS, Northrop and Lockheed hold program-embedded CDS and sole-source IDIQs; Booz Allen and Microsoft hold the ZT reference deployments. The buyer rarely re-competes.

ABAC only works if attributes mean the same thing across DoD PKI, service directories, cloud tenants and coalition authorities; every service runs its own ICAM and ZT program, so semantics and APIs diverge.

DoD CIO sets policy but does not buy; DISA, each service CIO, PEOs and combatant commands each own pieces; coalition sharing additionally depends on national policies (NATO ACCS integration took over two decades).

OpenTDF (2021-2024), ZTDF, NSA ZIGs (Jan 2026), cATO guidance and policy-as-code engines make source-tagging and continuous evidence practical only now; Flank Speed's target-level certification (Oct 2024) is the first proof that the enterprise half is achievable.

CDS procurement lines are small (CDES roughly $1-2M/yr) and unit volumes low; the money is in integration services and platform programs, not in software licenses, which discourages venture-backed entrants.
Enterprise ZTNA/identity for connected users is largely solved by Thunderdome and Flank Speed using commercial stacks; that sub-layer is not startup whitespace.

Automated, dominance-aware releasability on machine-generated tactical data and ZT enforcement in DDIL remain open; demonstrations recur annually (Bold Quest, CWIX, JS J6 assessments) without a program of record.

attractiveness.bull: The FY27 target-level deadline, NSA's Jan 2026 implementation guidelines, NGC2's scale-up and Joint Staff's coalition data-centric-security demos create a 2026-2028 window where every program office needs data tagging, ABAC policy and ZT evidence tooling. Open standards (OpenTDF/ZTDF, ACP-240) let a two-person team build an unclassified prototype in weeks; DEVCOM C5ISR has issued a named RFI for tactical data-in-use security; accredited hosting (Game Warden, JWCC marketplace) shortens ATO; and the pain is documented in GAO, Army journals and DAU webinars rather than only vendor marketing.
attractiveness.bear: The layer's value concentrates exactly where a student startup cannot go: classified enclaves, NSA-assessed CDS, coalition policy. Enterprise ZT and ICAM are already delivered by Booz Allen, Microsoft and large integrators with sole-source follow-ons; ZT compliance tooling is crowded; data tagging demand is real but the buyer has been 'demonstrating' it since 2022 without a program of record; one non-U.S.-person founder blocks clearances and complicates export control and FOCI; and revenue in CDS is low-volume and services-heavy.
attractiveness.verdict: Selectively attractive: pursue only the unclassified, standards-based sub-problems (interoperable tagging/labeling automation for C2 data, offline-capable policy/key enforcement for DDIL, ZT evidence automation) as a wedge, with an explicit plan to partner with an accredited CDS or ZT integrator rather than becoming one. Avoid building a CDS, CSfC product or enterprise ICAM competitor.

candidate_gaps.technical_wedge_hypothesis: A releasability decision API (attributes in, allowed partner set and required transforms out) that integrators embed in MPE chat/COP tools, built on ACP-240 and NATO labels.
candidate_gaps.mvp_sketch: Unclassified demo with synthetic partner attribute authorities and marking rules; integrate with Mattermost or TAK in a coalition exercise sandbox.
candidate_gaps.data_requirement: Partner attribute schemas, disclosure policy encodings (mostly classified/controlled).
candidate_gaps.integration_requirement: SAML/OIDC federation, MPE application APIs, CDS metadata.
candidate_gaps.entry_vehicle: Subcontract to MPE integrator; Bold Quest/CWIX; NATO DIANA (Second Front hosts DIANA at NATO UNCLASSIFIED).

candidate_gaps.killer_risk: Policy, not technology, is the bottleneck; a student startup cannot influence national disclosure policy.

candidate_gaps.title: Zero-trust evidence and continuous-authorization automation for program offices (91 target activities, ZT Overlays, NSA ZIG phases)
candidate_gaps.problem_one_sentence: Program offices must prove target-level ZT by 30 Sep 2027 against 91 activities and 400 pages of overlays, but evidence is assembled manually from heterogeneous tools.
candidate_gaps.user: ISSMs, program ZT leads, authorizing officials, DoD CIO ZT PfMO assessors
candidate_gaps.current_workflow: 1) Map system controls to ZT Overlays in spreadsheets/eMASS; 2) collect screenshots and logs from IdP, EDR, SIEM; 3) self-assess activity status; 4) PfMO review; 5) repeat annually.
candidate_gaps.current_solution: Integrator assessments (Booz Allen, Deloitte, GDIT), GRC tools (Xacta, RegScale), eMASS; Navy and DISA built their own evidence pipelines.
candidate_gaps.failure_point: Manual, non-continuous, inconsistent across components; brownfield systems lack telemetry.

candidate_gaps.why_startups_havent_solved: It is being solved, by integrators and GRC vendors; the buyer prefers services; differentiation is thin.
candidate_gaps.technical_wedge_hypothesis: Open telemetry-to-ZT-activity mapping (OSCAL) with connectors to Entra/Okta, EDR and SIEM producing continuous activity status.
candidate_gaps.mvp_sketch: OSCAL-based ZT activity tracker with a few connectors, piloted with one program office.
candidate_gaps.entry_vehicle: SBIR under DoD CIO/DISA, subcontract to assessment integrator.
candidate_gaps.killer_risk: Commoditized by integrators; low willingness to pay for software vs services.

candidate_gaps.title: Low-SWaP 'cross domain at the edge' / software-defined CDS for tactical units (J-rated for this founding team)
candidate_gaps.problem_one_sentence: Tactical units need faster, cheaper cross-domain movement of new data types (voice, video, FMV, ML outputs) than the current NCDSMO-baselined guards provide.
candidate_gaps.user: Tactical CDS operators, platform program offices, expeditionary targeting cells
candidate_gaps.current_workflow: 1) Program identifies new data type; 2) requests filter from CDS vendor; 3) vendor develops and NSA assesses; 4) years later the filter fields via sole-source modification.
candidate_gaps.current_solution: GDMS TACDS, Owl voice/video/FMV CDS, Everfox guards, PMAT Tactical Edge Nodes; DISA CDES for enterprise.
candidate_gaps.failure_point: Accreditation throughput and vendor lock; new filters arrive via sole-source IDIQs.

evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: TACDS 3.0 filter industry day (Dec 2025) indicates continued demand for new tactical filters
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: NSA RTB applies to all CDS protecting classified information and all CDS sold for export; only NCDSMO-listed solutions may be used (NIST AC-4(20))
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.label: FACT

candidate_gaps.why_startups_havent_solved: Certification, classification, export control, hardware assurance and incumbent sole-source vehicles; venture economics do not fit 3-5 year accreditation cycles.
candidate_gaps.technical_wedge_hypothesis: None recommended for a two-student team with a non-U.S.-person founder; the only plausible adjacency is supplying filter/data-format descriptions (DFDL) or tagging metadata to incumbents.
candidate_gaps.killer_risk: Cannot obtain NCDSMO listing or clearances.
